summary: Atlas resource tags are case-sensitive key-value pairs added to projects and clusters; Atlas copies cluster tags onto billing output (a Tag/<key> column in the invoice CSV and a tags field on Admin API invoice line items) so teams can build showback or chargeback reports, but tags are read when the CSV is generated or the API is called, so retagging mid-cycle rewrites the invoice view and clusters deleted before the export appear untagged. The FinOps Framework frames the same practice as allocation (apportioning costs to those responsible for them), built on an allocation strategy, a tagging strategy and a shared-cost strategy. This pack draws on 7 source pages across 4 host labels and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, parameters, how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history.

facts.text: The FinOps Framework defines allocation as apportioning costs to those responsible for them. Resource-level naming conventions and tags make that finer-grained. The strategy decides whether costs go to showback (to teams), chargeback (to finance) or cost-center allocation. Reports should surface spend not covered by the allocation metadata, and shared costs are split by a stated model (proportional, fixed or even). Tagging works better with automation and infrastructure as code.

Atlas resource tags are key-value pairs added to projects and clusters. Limits: 50 tags per cluster, keys and values up to 255 characters each, unique keys, and each tag value on at most 1,000 resources. Keys and values are case-sensitive, so environment and Environment are different keys.

We are excited to introduce MongoDB Atlas' new resource tagging functionality. You can now organize and manage Atlas resources with improved efficiency by applying tags to categorize database deployments based on your business needs. In turn, you are empowered to better work with various tools and integrations within your technology stack in order to analyze costs, monitor resource consumption, and automate workflows at scale.

Tags are key-value pairs that associate with a resource to provide additional context. For example, tagging a cluster with the key environment and value production would help to identify this cluster as being deployed to production. A tag can only have one value for a given key, on a particular resource. Therefore, this cluster could not have another tag with the key environment and the value production.

The Atlas Architecture Center's FinOps path combines four mechanisms. Tags give cost allocation by department, project or cost center. The pending-invoices Admin API feeds external FinOps tools. Cross-organization billing gives one paying organization visibility across linked organizations. MongoDB Charts billing dashboards accept tag-based charts and filters. Cost Explorer groups only by organization, project, cluster and service, not by tag.

In the invoice CSV, Atlas adds one column per tag key with the header Tag/<your key>, and the cell holds the tag value. The Admin API returns the tags in the results.lineItems.tags field of the Return All Pending Invoices for One Organization endpoint.

The endpoints response body contains the results.lineItems.tags field, which reflect the tags you applied to your resources (such as organizations and clusters). Invoice tags reflect the tag configuration at the moment the CSV is generated or the API is called. If a team retags a resource mid-billing-cycle, the whole invoice shows only the latest tags. Showback and chargeback reports must therefore treat tags as a snapshot, not a history.
Atlas stores tag values in plain text. Billing can read them, and Atlas sends cluster tags to the Datadog and Prometheus integrations. Tags must not hold PII or PHI.

Resource tags assigned to Atlas clusters are not preserved in invoices if the cluster is deleted before the invoice is exported. Atlas fetches tags live at export time rather than recording them when the cost is incurred. This means that any ephemeral cluster - correctly tagged throughout its entire lifetime - will appear as untagged in the invoice, making it impossible to attribute its costs to the right team, project, or cost center.

Resource tags in invoices should reflect the state at the time of use, not export time. Atlas should record and persist resource tags at the time each cost event occurs, so that invoice exports always reflect the tag state that was true during the billing period - regardless of whether the cluster still exists at the time of download. This is consistent with how cost allocation tagging works in AWS and GCP.
